paragraphs.text: This is the story of the Darling family. It is also the story of Peter Pan, a boy who may or may not exist—depending on how old you are.

The Darlings lived at Number 14, a house in London, England, near Kensington Gardens. At first, the family was just Mr. George Darling and his wife, Mrs. Darling. But then their children were born. Wendy came first, then John, and then Michael. Later, Nana came to live with them. She was the children’s nanny and made sure they were all well-cared for. Nana was a large, no-nonsense Newfoundland dog, who slept on the nursery floor.

Mr. Darling was a good father and an excellent provider. During the day, he worked in the city as a banker, encouraging people to spend money wisely. He liked to work with numbers at home too. Mr. Darling counted how much money the children cost him. How much would he have to spend on their milk and cookies? How much money would he spend on their shirts and coats? When the children caught the German measles or the mumps, he worried about the cost of medicine. But he and Mrs. Darling agreed that the children were worth every penny spent.

Mrs. Darling was more concerned about her children’s minds than about money. She was a lovely lady with a sweet mouth and a romantic sense of the world. Her mind was like a puzzle with many boxes, each one inside the other. Mrs. Darling thought about deep things. She worried about how her children were growing up. She knew from her own experience that when a child reaches the age of two, childhood is beginning to end.

As a young girl, Mrs. Darling had many suitors. All of them wanted to marry her. But George Darling, who was a young man at the time, asked her first. He was very smart. One day, while the other boys were walking to her house to propose, Mr. Darling took a taxi. He got there ahead of the others and won her love. She happily gave him all her kisses, except for one. This kiss was her little secret. She saved it in the right corner of her sweet mouth for a special occasion.

When Mrs. Darling was busy, Nana took care of the children. Nana was a treasure. Every morning, she walked the children in single file to Miss Fulsom’s kindergarten school. When they were well-behaved, Nana walked quietly by their side. When they were naughty, she barked and pushed them back into line with her huge head. She always carried an umbrella in her mouth, just in case of rain.

Mr. Darling hired Nana as a nanny because she was much cheaper than a person. Even though the neighbors might gossip about a dog working as a nanny, the idea made perfect sense to Mr. Darling. Before Nana picked up the children from school, she waited in the basement with the other nannies. They complained about having a dog among them, and the neighbors did talk, but the Darlings didn’t care.

Before bedtime, there was always much merriment at Number 14. The children were allowed to sing and dance before going to bed. Oh, the dances were such fun! Nana barked in time with the music. The other servant, Liza, danced too. Mr. Darling watched alone and apart on the sidelines. But Mrs. Darling joined the children and spun around wildly. And sometimes she even planted her secret kiss on the cheek of one of the children.
Yes, the Darling family lived very happily together—until the coming of Peter Pan.

Mothers always worry about what their children are thinking. Sometimes, they imagine traveling through the minds of their sleeping children. They like to tidy up their children’s thoughts for the next morning. It is like straightening up a chest of drawers. A mother folds her child’s naughtiness into a small place in the back of the drawer. The better thoughts are kept in the front of the drawer, ready to be brought out the following morning.

When Mrs. Darling traveled through her children’s minds, she found the words "Peter" and "Neverland." Though she couldn’t quite place the names, they seemed strangely familiar to her. Mrs. Darling thought they might be from her own childhood. But now that she was a grown-up, it was hard to remember exactly what the words meant. She vaguely recalled that Peter was a little boy who lived with the fairies. He lived on an island called Neverland, the land of dreams. Every child dreams about adventures in Neverland. But Mrs. Darling, as an adult, knew that these adventures were never true.
One morning, Mrs. Darling found some stray leaves on the nursery floor just inside the nursery window. "How did these leaves get here?" she asked the children.
"Some nights, Peter comes to visit," Wendy replied. "Peter is very naughty. He never cleans up after himself. He probably dropped the leaves and forgot to pick them up before he left."

When Mrs. Darling asked Wendy to tell her more about Peter, Wendy described his visits. "He comes in through the window of our nursery. He sits at the foot of my bed and sometimes plays his flute." Unfortunately, Wendy explained, she was always asleep during Peter’s visits. She didn’t know how she knew about them. She just knew that Peter had surely been there.

Mrs. Darling thought Wendy was only describing her dreams. The nursery was on the third floor and a very long way from the ground. How could anyone possibly come through the window? This story couldn’t be real.

But the leaves that she found on the nursery floor were certainly real. Mrs. Darling looked at them carefully. They were unusual leaves, certainly not found anywhere in England. The veins of the leaves formed a fine skeleton of lines.

The following evening was Nana’s night off. While the dog went out on the town, Mrs. Darling bathed her children and tucked them into bed. Then she sang to Wendy, John, and Michael, until they each fell asleep. Mrs. Darling sat down by the fire in the nursery and did her sewing. She loved to watch the children while they slept. They looked so peaceful. She, too, soon fell asleep.
As she slept, Mrs. Darling had a dream about Neverland. She dreamed that a strange boy had flown far away from his home. What a strange dream for a grown-up to have!

All of a sudden, the nursery window blew open. A boy dressed in the same skeleton leaves flew in, lightly touching down on the floor. Following him was a strange light no bigger than someone’s fist. The light darted around the room as if it were alive. It was light as dust—fairy dust.

Mrs. Darling recognized the boy. He was Peter Pan. And he was just as young as he had been when she first saw him as a little girl. She remembered him now. His tiny teeth sparkled like small pearls. At the sight of him, Mrs. Darling let out a scream.

Just then, Nana returned from her evening out and burst into the nursery, barking. She growled and sprang at Peter, who leapt lightly up to the window. But before he could escape, Nana grabbed Peter’s shadow in her mouth. As Peter flew away, his shadow tore off from his body.
Concerned for Peter, Mrs. Darling ran outside and down the street to look for him. But all she saw was a shooting star in the sky.

The next night started as an ordinary Friday evening, even though it was the last time Mr. and Mrs. Darling saw their three children for a very long time. They were dressing for a dinner party, and Mrs. Darling was helping her husband tie his bow tie. She looked splendid in her white evening gown and a necklace George had given her. She told her husband about seeing Peter in the nursery the night before. When she described how Nana had caught his shadow, Mr. Darling laughed at the story. But when she took him to the nursery and showed him the shadow, which she had carefully folded and put in a drawer, he almost believed her.

Meanwhile, Nana was getting the children ready for bed. As the baby of the family, Michael sometimes made a fuss. "I won’t take a bath! I won’t! And I won’t go to bed!" he would shout. Tonight, when it came time for his medicine, Michael refused to take it.

Michael ran from the bathroom into the nursery, and Nana followed with his spoonful of medicine held carefully between her teeth. John and Wendy were right behind. When Mr. and Mrs. Darling saw the problem, Mrs. Darling went straight to the kitchen for a chocolate to sweeten the taste of the medicine.
Mr. Darling was much more strict. "Be brave!" he commanded Michael. "When I was your age, I took medicine without a word. I even thanked my parents for giving me medicine to make me well."

Trying to be helpful, Wendy interrupted, "You still take medicine too, don’t you, Father?" It was true. And even though Mr. Darling wanted Michael to be brave, it was also true that he didn’t like his medicine. He often found reasons not to take it.

"It’s much nastier than Michael’s!" he said. "And, if I hadn’t lost the bottle, I would take it now to show you how I do it, Michael." In fact, Mr. Darling hadn’t actually lost the medicine. He had hidden the bottle at the back of the medicine cabinet.

"I know where it is, Father," said Wendy. She was always a helpful daughter. "I’ll bring it to you." She ran off before he could stop her. Wendy returned with the medicine in a glass. It was a white liquid that looked like milk.
Mr. Darling shuddered when he saw it. "Michael first," he said.
"Father first," responded Michael.
"It isn’t fair," Mr. Darling complained. "There is more medicine in my glass than in Michael’s spoon."
"Father, I am waiting for you," said Michael suspiciously.
Wendy made a suggestion. "Why not take your medicines at the same time?" She counted to three: "One, two, three, go!"
Michael took his medicine, but Mr. Darling hid his glass behind his back.
Michael let out a yell. "Not fair!"
Wendy cried, "Oh Father, I can’t believe you did that!"
"Well, I meant to take mine, but I . . . I missed it," Father said.
John looked at his father sadly, and Nana left the room in disgust.

Mr. Darling knew he had disappointed his children. He didn’t like the way they were looking at him. "Let’s play a joke on Nana," he suggested. "I will pour my medicine into Nana’s bowl. She will think it is milk. What fun!" he said, trying to be playful as he poured the medicine.
When Nana returned, he patted her on the head.
"Good dog," he said. "Have a little milk from your bowl, Nana."

Nana wagged her tail and began to lap up the liquid. The children were shocked at their father’s sense of humor. They didn’t think his joke was funny at all. When the medicine was all gone, Nana shook her big head and crept into her doghouse to lie down. She did not look well.
Mrs. Darling came back to a silent room. She looked at the unhappy group and the sick dog. Then she picked up Nana’s bowl and sniffed it.
"George, it’s your medicine! How could you!" she cried.
The children and Mrs. Darling were comforting Nana with pats and cuddles. Nana’s stomach was upset from drinking Mr. Darling’s medicine.

"It was only a joke," Mr. Darling said. It was clear that nobody had any sympathy for him, and this upset him. "All you care about is that dog. What about my feelings?" he shouted. Then he said, "The proper place for a dog is tied up in the yard!" To prove his point, Mr. Darling dragged Nana from the nursery. He pulled her outside and chained her to a tree in the backyard.

Suddenly ashamed, he sat down on the back steps and cried. He knew he had made a mistake, but Mr. Darling could not give in. He couldn’t face his family if he had to admit that he was wrong. So, that night, Nana was left in the backyard, away from the nursery.
Mrs. Darling put the kids to bed. They could all hear Nana barking outside. John whimpered, "Poor Nana. She sounds so unhappy."
But Wendy was wiser. "That is not Nana’s unhappy bark. It’s how she barks when she smells danger."

Mrs. Darling checked the nursery window to make sure it was properly shut. "Oh, how I wish I weren’t going to a dinner party tonight!" she thought to herself. She was worried about leaving the children in the nursery without Nana to watch them. "The night lights will keep you from harm," she told the children. She tucked each child into bed. She sang each a song. She kissed them good night on their eyelids and, with that, she left the nursery.

Then Mr. and Mrs. Darling went out into the night. They didn’t have far to go. The dinner party was at Number 27, only a few yards away from their house. It had been snowing, and they were the only people in the street. The stars shone down on the soft white covering of snow and on the couple. But as soon as the door of Number 27 closed behind them, the stars, who were friends of Peter Pan, whispered, "Go now, Peter!"

Back in the nursery, Wendy, John, and Michael had fallen asleep. A bright light darted from one dresser drawer to another. It was not really a light, though. When it rested for a moment, you could see it was a fairy no larger than a hand. The fairy’s name was Tinker Bell. A perfect miniature figure, she was beautifully dressed in a tiny leaf. She had found a way into the nursery to look for Peter’s shadow.
Suddenly the window blew open, and Peter flew into the nursery.

"Tinker Bell," he called softly, "where are you?" He had carried the fairy part of the way from Neverland, and her fairy dust was still all over his hands. "Come and help me find my shadow!" Peter said.
The ring of a tiny bell answered him. This was Tinker Bell’s fairy language.

When Tinker Bell explained that his shadow was in the dresser, Peter rummaged through all the drawers, spilling everything all over the floor. He made a terrible mess, but he didn’t notice. He also didn’t notice that he accidentally locked Tinker Bell in one of the drawers.

Finally, Peter found his shadow. He was delighted. But how could he attach it to himself again? Peter put the shadow on the floor and lay down on it. But it wouldn’t stick to his body. Next he tried to glue it on with soap from the bathroom. But this didn’t work either. Frustrated, Peter sat down and cried.

Wendy was awakened by Peter’s crying. She wasn’t very frightened to see the strange boy sitting on the nursery floor. Instead she was curious about him. She had almost expected him to be there. "Boy," she asked softly, "what is your name and why are you crying?"

Forgetting his own troubles for the moment, Peter got up from the floor and bowed graciously. He knew how to act properly when he wanted to. "Let me introduce myself," he said. "I’m Peter Pan. What’s your name?"
"I’m Wendy Darling," replied Wendy. "Where do you come from?"
"I live at the second star to the right, and then straight on till morning," Peter said.
"What a funny address. Is that where you get mail?"
"I don’t get any mail."
"But your mother must get mail."
"I don’t have a mother," said Peter.
"I’m so sorry you don’t have a mother," Wendy said sympathetically.
"That’s not why I’m upset," said Peter. "I’m upset because I can’t get my shadow to stick back on me."
"I can fix that," Wendy answered helpfully. She went to get the sewing kit and sewed the shadow onto Peter’s feet. When she was done, his shadow was as good as new.

Peter gave a howl of delight. "How clever I am!" he crowed, jumping about. He had already forgotten that it was Wendy who had solved his problem. Wendy reminded him of her part in his good fortune. So he replied, "Wendy, one girl is more useful than twenty boys." He didn’t want to offend her.
Touched by his sweet words, Wendy offered to give him a kiss. But Peter didn’t understand what a kiss was. Suddenly becoming shy, Wendy handed him a thimble instead.
"Now I will give you a kiss too," Peter said. Thinking a kiss was a present, he dropped a button in the shape of an acorn into her hand. Wendy put the button on a chain around her neck.
"I promise to wear this forever," she said. Wendy asked Peter how old he was.
"I’m still very young," said Peter. "I didn’t want to ever grow up, so I ran away when I was born. I went to live with the fairies."

Wendy wanted to know everything about fairies and asked many questions. Peter explained that when the first baby ever born laughed for the first time, its laugh broke into a thousand pieces. The pieces all went skipping around, and that was the beginning of fairies.

He also said there should be one fairy for every boy and girl, but children grow old too soon. "And they stop believing in fairies," said Peter. "Each time a child says ‘I don’t believe in fairies,’ a fairy dies."
While he was speaking of fairies, Peter suddenly remembered Tinker Bell, who had been quiet all this time. When he called her name, a tinkling sound came from the chest of drawers.
"What’s that? It sounds like bells," said Wendy.

"That’s Tinker Bell, my fairy friend. I think I accidentally shut her in the drawer," Peter laughed. When he opened the drawer, Tinker Bell darted from place to place. She screamed angry words that only Peter could understand.
"You shouldn’t say such naughty things!" he responded.
Wendy was totally delighted that there was a fairy in her nursery. When Tinker Bell finally stood still on the cuckoo clock, Wendy cried, "Oh she’s so lovely!"
Tinker Bell replied something in fairy language. Then she disappeared into the bathroom.
"What is she saying, Peter?" Wendy asked.
"Tink says you are an ugly girl," he replied, a bit too honestly. "You see, she is a common fairy and isn’t very polite."
Wendy continued to question Peter about himself. "If you don’t live with your mother, who do you live with?"
Peter told her that he lived with the Lost Boys. They were children who had fallen out of their strollers as infants. These boys had been taken to Neverland, where Peter was their captain.

He continued, "Sadly, we are all boys, with no girls around. And sometimes we get very lonely. For instance, there is no one to tell us stories. That’s why I sometimes come to your nursery and listen to your stories. The other night your mother was telling such a lovely story about the lady with the glass slippers."
"Peter, that was Cinderella. And her prince found her and they lived happily ever after," Wendy explained.
Peter was so excited that he rose and hurried to the window.
"Where are you going?" Wendy cried.
"To tell the other boys the end of that story."
"Don’t go, Peter," she pleaded. "I know so many other stories. Oh, the stories I could tell you and the Lost Boys!"
When he heard this, Peter hurried back to her with a greedy look in his eyes.
Peter pleaded with Wendy to come with him to Neverland. "I’ll teach you to fly, and then we can fly there together," he said. "There are mermaids there too! Have you ever seen a mermaid?"
"Mermaids!" cried Wendy. She was very excited about going, but she was worried about leaving the rest of her family.

"You can tell the Lost Boys and me lots of stories," begged Peter. "Then you can tuck us into bed at night. None of us has ever been tucked in before. You can sew and make pockets for us. You see, none of our clothing has any pockets. We really could use a girl in Neverland, Wendy."
Wendy loved the idea of taking care of Peter and his Lost Boys. Bravely, she tried to give him a kiss on his cheek again. But when she bent over to kiss him, she suddenly screamed with pain.
"It feels as if someone is pinching me," she cried.
"That must be Tink," said Peter. "I never saw her act so naughtily with a stranger before."
Tinker Bell darted around the room.
"She says she will pinch you again each time you do that," Peter said. He could not understand why, but Wendy understood. Tinker Bell was jealous!
Wendy changed the subject. "Can you teach John and Michael to fly, too?"
"If you like," Peter answered. For Wendy’s sake, he was willing to put up with her brothers.
Wendy shook her brothers, who were still asleep in their beds. "Wake up, John! Wake up, Michael! Peter is here, and he is going to teach us to fly."
The boys got up, excited. "Can Peter really fly?" John asked, as he put on the black top hat he liked to wear. Peter didn’t say anything. He just flew around the room gracefully. It looked so easy.
"How do you do it?" asked John. He jumped off the bed and landed on his backside.
"You just think wonderful thoughts," Peter explained, "and they lift you up in the air."

But what Peter didn’t say was that people can’t fly unless fairy dust has been blown on them. Fortunately, Peter still had some fairy dust on his hands from Tinker Bell. He blew some magic dust on each of the children.
"Just wiggle your shoulders and think lovely thoughts," he instructed.
Michael was first, and immediately he floated up in the air. "Look at me, I’m flying!" he shouted.

Then John and Wendy tried it. They were not as graceful as Peter, but each was able to fly across the room. Their heads bobbed against the ceiling. John had to hold onto his hat to keep it from being knocked off. Up and down they went, and round and round.
"With a little more practice, you’ll be able to fly with me to Neverland. You’ll see the pirates and wild animals!" said Peter, tempting the boys.
"Hooray—pirates!" cried John.
"Hooray—wild animals!" shouted Michael.

Meanwhile Nana, who was tied up in the backyard, kept barking. Liza, the servant, was preparing pudding in the kitchen. She was getting very annoyed; Nana had been barking all night. Liza stepped outside to check on her.
"If you don’t stop barking, I will have to fetch the master and mistress at Number 27," scolded Liza. "I’ll bring them home from the party to punish you."

This gave Nana an idea. She would get the Darlings herself! The dog quieted down on purpose. Then, when Liza returned to the kitchen, Nana pulled at her chain hard. It broke in two. She burst out of the yard, crossed the street, and ran into Number 27. Once she was inside, she waved her paws in the air. Now Mr. and Mrs. Darling knew that something terrible was happening at their house. Without saying good-bye to their hostess, they rushed into the street. When they reached their house, they looked up and saw the nursery’s open window.
By the time Mr. and Mrs. Darling ran up to the nursery, the children—Wendy, John, and Michael—had flown away with Peter.

"Second star to the right and then straight on till morning." That was how Peter had described the way to the island of Neverland. But these directions were not very exact. And the children had no map! They were depending on Peter to guide them there.

At first, they were excited as he led them through the clouds. They flew over treetops, made rings around tall buildings, and dipped close to the waves in the sea. From the sky, the world looked very different and their eyes delighted in everything.

"Follow me!" Peter commanded. He used his best captain’s voice. But Peter was a little too daring. He flew a little too close to the trees―just missing their branches. He flew a little too close to the water—touching every shark’s tail. As the children flew with Peter, night became day, light became dark; then it became light, then dark again. The moon and the sun took turns trading places. The children followed Peter bravely.

But the excitement of flying started to wear off. The children became hungry and cold. They also became sleepy, and this was dangerous. In order to fly, they had to remain awake. When Michael suddenly nodded off, he began to fall.

"There he goes—down, down, down!" Peter laughed. He thought this was hilarious, but Wendy was alarmed. Peter caught Michael just before he fell into the sea. When he saw how upset Wendy was, he taught the children how to rest on a cloud.

Peter flew much faster than the others. Sometimes he would fly out of sight for a while. He had secret adventures on his own. He would come back talking about a star or a fairy he had met. When he was out on an adventure, Wendy worried that he might forget them altogether!
"What would we do if Peter were to leave us?" asked John.
"Well, we would have to go on. We don’t know how to stop," replied Wendy, trying to sound brave. This was true. Peter had not shown them how to stop flying.
Soon they lost track of time. How long had they been traveling? Would they ever arrive in Neverland? The children wondered whether they had lost their way.
Finally, they saw an island in the distance. The island seemed to be calling to them. It was all very new and strange—yet somehow familiar at the same time.
"There it is," said Peter, "where all the arrows are pointing."
He was right. A hundred golden arrows, sent by the setting sun, pointed to the magic shore of Neverland. Night was approaching. The sun wanted to make sure they found their way safely.

The children looked down below. They could see splashes of color everywhere. Purple mountains stood behind dark green forests. Rivers and lakes ran through the green land like blue veins. Red coral reefs accented the color of the water. Flowers and bushes in brilliant shades dotted the landscape of Neverland.

Strangely, the children immediately recognized the island. Below them, they each saw a landscape from their own dreams. John saw his lake with flamingos. Michael saw his cave with a river running through it. And Wendy saw Mermaid Lagoon, just as she had often dreamed of it.

In the nursery, Neverland had been make-believe, part of a dream world. Now that they were here, it was all very real. The sun’s golden arrows disappeared; the sky became dark. Night was falling on Neverland, and suddenly the children were frightened. There were no nursery night-lights to keep them safe. Nana wasn’t standing guard beside them. Still flying, they all moved closer to Peter.
Suddenly Peter was not as carefree as he had been. He was now on the alert. He looked down in the growing darkness and pointed to the smoke rising from a campfire below.

"See that smoke? It comes from the camp of the Indians just across the Mysterious River." Peter explained to the children. "Those are smoke signals. They are on the war path. And look," he said, pointing to another part of the island. "There are the pirates getting ready to shoot their cannon, called Long Tom, at Execution Dock. We need to be on our guard."
With this, Peter sent Tinker Bell up front to lead the way. Her glow provided enough light for everyone to see each other and the land below.

All had been quiet in Neverland while Peter was gone. When Peter was not there, life on the island was always more peaceful. The fairies and mermaids even took an extra hour to get up in the morning. Rather than fighting, the pirates and the Lost Boys just made faces at each other when they met. The Indians planted their corn, and the wild animals looked after their young. But when Peter arrived, the action began!

Peter told the children about the pirates and their ship, the Jolly Roger . Their eyes lit up when he talked about the pirates’ wicked leader—Captain Hook! The children had heard of him and his evil reputation. Michael began to cry.
John asked, "Is he as mean and as big as they say?"
"Well, he’s a bit smaller now," replied Peter, "because I cut off his right hand."
"Then he can’t fight?" replied Michael hopefully.
"Oh no, he can fight. He’s as fierce as ever. But now he has an iron hook instead of a right hand. In fact, he’s been known to claw people to death with that hook."
"Well, I wonder what it would be like to meet him!" said John. He was almost looking forward to a pirate adventure.
"Not me, I would be too scared!" cried Michael.
"As captain, there is one thing I demand of each boy who serves under me," said Peter. "If we meet Hook in a fight, you must leave him to me."
"Ay, ay, sir," replied both boys.
"But right now, we aren’t ready for a fight," Peter declared. "Let’s get out of sight. The pirates might already have seen us because of Tink’s light."
"Tell her to put out her light," the children cried in unison.
"Her light only goes out when she is asleep," said Peter. "But we can put her in John’s top hat."

When Tinker Bell thought Peter would carry the hat, she agreed happily. But when Peter gave the hat to Wendy, Tink was upset. After thinking about it, the fairy decided not to make a fuss—at least not just yet.
With Tinker Bell in the hat, the group’s guiding light was gone. They flew on in complete silence. Suddenly, Peter and the children became enveloped in a ghostly stillness.
"If only something would make a sound . . ." sighed Michael.

As if to answer Michael’s wish, there was a huge boom ! The pirates had fired Long Tom into the sky. The cannon’s roar echoed through the mountains and sent the group flying in different directions. No one was hit, but Peter was thrown far out to sea. Wendy was blown upward. She still held John’s hat with Tinker Bell in it.

Tinker Bell wasn’t a bad fairy. Sometimes she was really good. But at this moment, she was bad. She hated Wendy because she was jealous of Wendy’s feelings for Peter. It would have been better for Wendy if she had dropped the hat, but Wendy would never have let go.

After the cannon blast, Tinker Bell popped out of the hat and tinkled something in fairy language. Wendy did not understand. She assumed the fairy was saying "Follow me." What else could Wendy do? She followed.

The Lost Boys were walking through the woods. They were hoping to greet their captain, Peter Pan, after his trip to the nursery. But while the Lost Boys were looking for Peter, the pirates were looking for the Lost Boys. Meanwhile, the Indians were looking for the pirates. And the wild animals were looking for the Indians. It was like a grand march. Everyone was going round and round the island, ready to fight if they met. But they did not meet because they were all walking at the same speed!

The Lost Boys were dressed in bear skins and had their daggers ready. There were six of them, and they were all very sweet. But they could be wild at times. Of course, they were all very young. Whenever one of them began to grow up, Peter quickly sent that boy away. It was against the rules to grow up in Neverland.

As the march continued, each boy was firmly on the lookout. Tootles was brave. But he always seemed to miss the fighting when a battle broke out. Adventures would always happen just when he stepped around a corner to gather a few sticks of firewood. When he’d return, the other boys would be covered in blood and the enemy would be gone. He was the easiest boy to trick. Everyone knew this—including Tinker Bell. Handsome Nibs was followed by Slightly, the boldest boy of the group.
"I am the only one not afraid of pirates," Slightly boasted. But no one ever believed him.

Curly, who always got into trouble for something—even when he hadn’t done it, was the fourth in line. And last were the twins. They looked so much alike that even Peter couldn’t tell one from the other. The twins didn’t talk much.

The pirates followed right behind the Lost Boys—right in their footsteps! As the pirates walked through the trees, they bragged about their latest adventures. The men were laughing and singing loud pirate songs. Huge and handsome Cecco wore coins in his ears. Bill Jukes had tattoos all over his body. Cookson was said to be the son of a famous pirate. Bloodthirsty Gentleman Starkey once worked in a public school. The bandits Skylights, Robert Mullins, and Alf Mason also belonged to the pirate crew. All three of them were famous on the high seas. Pirate Noodler had hands that looked as if they were on backwards. Finally, there was friendly Smee. His job was to look after the pirate ship and Captain Hook.

In front of the line, sitting in a chariot pulled by his men, was Captain James Hook. He yelled orders at his men as if they were dogs. Hook was handsome, with long black curls and deep blue eyes. In fact, the man was very fashionable. He wore a starched lace collar under his splendid red jacket. His tall black boots shone because Smee polished them every day. The captain always had a cigar hanging from his lip. The Indians followed the boot marks of the pirates. They moved silently down the path carrying their tomahawks. Their bodies were shiny with paint and oil. Braided around their necks was the hair of pirates they had killed. The Indians didn’t say one word. Great Big Little Panther crept quietly on his hands and knees. Princess Tiger Lily walked proudly upright.

Next in the line of characters came the wild animals—lions, tigers, bears, and other beasts. Their tongues were hanging out with hunger. The animals were ready. They might catch a boy, a pirate, an Indian, or even one of their own. The last in line was a giant crocodile. He was looking for one victim only—Captain Hook.
The march might have gone on forever, but one of the groups stopped. It was the Lost Boys. They heard pirate laughter in the distance. And they heard a scary pirate song.
"Yo ho! Yo ho! The pirate life! The skull and bones! Hey, hey, they’ll go down to Davy Jones!"
"Davy Jones!" thought the boys. That meant the bottom of the ocean! The boys ran swiftly through the woods. They were quick as bunnies, returning to their home under the ground.

For many years, Hook and his pirates had searched for the hidden entrance to the Lost Boys’ home, but had never found it. As the pirates followed the boys, hoping to be led to the entrance, they saw Tootles. As always, Tootles was way behind the other boys, who had already disappeared into their hiding place.
The pirates were about to shoot him dead when Hook stopped them.

"If you fire your pistols now," he roared, "the Indians will find us. Do you want to lose your hair?" Meanwhile, Tootles had disappeared, and the pirates began to run back to their ship in fear of the Indians.

Alone with Smee, who had stayed behind, Hook calmed down and told his sad tale. "I want to catch all six boys at one time. But most of all I want their captain, Peter Pan. It was Peter Pan who cut off my hand." He shook his hook threateningly. "I’ve waited a long time to catch him with this."
"I’ve heard you say many times," said Smee, "that one hook is worth a dozen hands."

"Nonetheless, I want Peter. He flung my hand to a crocodile that was passing by. And the crocodile liked my hand so much that it has followed me ever since. On land and sea, it licks its lips, hoping for the rest of me. I can never relax."
"In a way that’s a compliment to you, Captain," said the loyal Smee.

"It’s Peter who gave the crocodile its taste for me," said Hook. "Luckily, that crocodile also swallowed a clock, so I always know by its ticking sound whenever it comes near. Without that warning, it would already have had me for supper."
"Someday that clock will break down," said Smee, "and you’ll be in big trouble."
"Yes, that’s my fear." Shuddering, Hook sat down on a giant mushroom for a moment. Suddenly he jumped up. "This seat is hot!"

Hook and Smee examined the giant mushroom. When Smee tried to pull it out of the ground, he found it had no roots. Furthermore, it had smoke coming out of it. They had discovered the chimney of the Lost Boys’ underground home.
Now they could hear the boys’ voices.
Smee whispered, "Did you hear them say Peter Pan will be back soon?"
"Good!" said Hook. "Let’s return to the ship and think of a way to capture him." But before they left, they heard one more thing. Tick-tock, tick-tock, tick-tock.
Hook gasped, "It’s the crocodile!" and he ran away. Smee quickly followed.

The boys had a clever way in and out of their underground home, and they used it to come out. Tootles, who had been hiding from the pirates in the woods, joined the rest of his friends. He was very excited. "I saw a wonderful thing in the sky! A great white bird! It’s flying this way."
"What kind of bird?" the others asked.
"I don’t know," replied Tootles, "but it looks almost like a girl. It flies as though it’s in pain, and it keeps crying ‘Poor Wendy’."
"I remember now," said Slightly. "I think there are birds called the Wendy Bird."

"Here it comes!" shouted Curly, pointing upward. They could hear Wendy’s cries—along with the tinkle of Tinker Bell. With Peter far away, Tinker Bell didn’t have to act nice anymore. She could do what she wanted. In the air, the jealous fairy had been pinching Wendy all over her body. Seeing the boys, she stopped.
"Hello, Tink!" yelled the boys.
Tinker Bell landed in a nearby tree. "Hello, boys. Peter wants you to shoot the Wendy Bird," she lied.
Never one to question Peter’s wishes, Tootles immediately aimed his bow and arrow. The others watched Wendy, who was still up in the sky.
"Peter will be so proud of you!" Tinker Bell said encouragingly.
Tootles fired, and Wendy fluttered to the ground, an arrow in her chest.
Tootles bragged to the other boys: "Aha! I have shot the Wendy Bird. Peter will be so proud of me."
"This is no bird," said Slightly. "It’s a girl!"
"Now I understand," said Curly. "Maybe Peter was bringing her here to take care of us."
"And you have killed her!" scolded Nibs.
Tootle’s face turned white when he realized his mistake.

He was now afraid of what Peter would say and of how he would be punished. It was a very tragic moment. All the boys looked down in deep regret and sorrow. Just then, they heard a crowing from up above.
This was Peter’s usual signal to the boys.
"It’s Peter!" the boys cried.
"We must hide her," whispered Nibs. Nodding, the others crowded around Wendy’s body in confusion.

"Greetings, boys," said Peter as he dropped down from the sky. "I have good news. I’ve brought a mother to take care of us all." He looked around at his boys. There were none of the usual salutes or cheers. "Why aren’t you cheering me?" he asked. "Why so sad?"
The boys stepped aside for Peter to see and then pointed to the body.
"She’s dead," said Peter, as he pulled the arrow from Wendy’s chest. "Who did this?"
When Tootles admitted his mistake, Peter raised his arm to hit him. But a small hand stopped him. Wendy wasn’t quite dead yet. Even in her weak state, she had protected Tootles.
"She lives!" the boys shouted with joy. Peter knelt beside her and found the acorn button he had given her. It was still on a chain around her neck. It had protected her from the arrow.
"That’s the kiss I gave her, and it has saved her life. I’m such a hero!" cried Peter.
"Hooray!" Now the boys had something to cheer about.
Only Tinker Bell was miserable. The boys told Peter what she had said to them.
"Tink, I’m ashamed of you!" said Peter. "Out of my sight! I don’t want to see you anymore."
Tinker Bell flew down and landed on Peter’s arm. She pleaded with him. But Wendy, still lying as if dead, raised her arm again.
Feeling a bit sorry for the fairy, Peter gave in. "Well, maybe I won’t banish you forever. But at least for a whole week!"
Even so, Tinker Bell was not the least bit grateful to Wendy. In fact, she wanted to pinch Wendy even more.
"Let’s carry Wendy down to the house," Curly suggested.
"But we shouldn’t touch her," said Tootles. "We might accidentally hurt her even more."
"If she lies here in the open overnight, she’ll die," argued Slightly.

"Well then, let’s build a temporary little house around her right here," suggested Peter. "Bring me the best of what each of you have. You can take it from our house," he ordered in his captain’s voice.

Happy to follow Peter’s orders again, the boys went about finding soft bedding, firewood, and anything else they could think of. They went up and down and all around, working hard to make their new mother comfortable.
Suddenly, John and Michael appeared in the sky. They too were relieved to see Peter again. "Hello, Peter!" they yelled.

"Hello," Peter replied. He had actually forgotten all about them. Peter was busy measuring Wendy to see how large the new house would need to be. John and Michael watched the frantic activity around them.
"Is Wendy asleep?" asked John, seeing his sister on the ground.
"Let’s wake her up," said Michael. "She can make our dinner."
"Yes, we’re hungry!" John shouted.
"Maybe later," said Peter. "Now you can help the others carry branches to build a house for your sister."
"A house for Wendy?" John exclaimed. "She’s only a girl."
"But she’s going to be our mother. We must be respectful and kind," explained Curly.

The forest came alive with the sound of the boys cutting and hammering. They had already carried up everything Wendy might need from their underground home—tables, chairs, a dresser, and a bed. Now they needed to build the walls.
"If only we knew the kind of house she likes," said Curly.
When Wendy began to wake up, they asked, "Wendy, tell us what kind of house you would like."
Opening her eyes, she began to sing:
I wish I had a pretty house,
The littlest ever seen,
With funny little red walls
And a roof of mossy green.
They were delighted to hear her voice. They brought moss for the roof, and branches with red sap for the walls of the little house. "What next?" they asked.
And she sang again:
Oh, next I’ll have
Blue windows all about,
With roses peeking in,
And children peeping out.
They carved out windows and made make-believe roses to decorate the outside of the windows. As for children, they would be her children.
The house was almost done. It looked beautiful, and the boys were very proud that they had made such a nice place for her. They loved Wendy already.
But once the walls were up around her, the boys couldn’t see her anymore. They stayed outside, wondering what to do.

"What we need now is a door and a knocker," said the practical Slightly. They shaped a door from a large piece of wood. Then Tootles gave up the bottom of his shoe, which made an excellent knocker. Now the house was truly finished. There was nothing to do now but knock on the door.
"We must all look our best," Peter told the boys. "First impressions are very important."

They washed their hands in a nearby stream and came back to the house. In the lead as always, Peter knocked politely on the door. The door opened and Wendy came out. She looked properly surprised—just how they had hoped she would look.
"Who are you?" she asked.
Slightly was the first to speak. "Wendy, we are the Lost Boys, and we have built this house for you."
"Oh, say that you’re pleased," cried Nibs excitedly.
"It’s a very lovely house! I thank you so much for your kindness," said Wendy. And that was just what they had hoped she would say.
"And we want to be your children," said Tootles shyly.
Then they all went down on their knees and cried, "Wendy, please be our mother."
"But I’m only a little girl," said Wendy, "and I have no real experience as a mother."
"Doesn’t matter," said Peter, who always knew best. "We just need a nice motherly type of person to help us."

"I will do my best," Wendy replied. With those words, she invited all the boys, including her brothers, inside. "Make sure to take off your shoes first," she instructed. "Then I’ll tell you a story before you go to bed. How would you like it if I told you the rest of the story of Cinderella?"
All the boys were delighted, even John and Michael. They squeezed into the tiny little house. And that was the first of many cozy evenings the boys spent with Wendy.

Later, when she felt better, she began to tuck them into their beds in the house underground. But for quite a long time, she slept in the little house the boys had lovingly made for her. Peter kept watch outside with his sword. Pirates, Indians, and beasts could be heard prowling in the distance.
And so they lived happily ever after—for a while.

As the pirates had discovered, there was no visible entrance to the boys’ underground home. Instead, there were seven separate doors. Seven hollow trees acted as tunnels. The tunnels fit each Lost Boy exactly. Each tree was the exact size of each boy, so they could easily slide in and out.

Peter measured Wendy, John, and Michael, so that they too could have their own hollow tree entrances. Unless the fit was perfect, it was difficult to slide up and down. Peter taught them to draw in their breath, and then wriggle down the hollow at just the right speed. Coming back up was much the same. After a few days' practice, they were going up and down easily.

Rough and simple, the underground home was little more than a cave. It was mostly one large room with a dirt floor. A huge fireplace stood in the middle of the room. The fire could be seen from anywhere in the room. Big fat mushrooms served as stools. A tree grew in one corner of the room. The boys sawed it down to floor level every morning. But every afternoon it grew about two feet high. They covered it with a door, and this served as their table. After supper, they would clear the table, take down the door, and saw off the trunk again. This way, they had more room to play and dance in the evenings.

A great big bed was tilted against the wall by day and set down at night. It filled nearly half the room. All the boys, except Michael, slept together and squished like sardines in a can. When one rolled over, they all rolled over. Michael was the youngest, so Wendy decided to hang a basket up for his bed.

It was hard taking care of nine active boys. Every day Wendy cooked for them. Sometimes it was real food collected by the boys during the day. Other times it was make-believe food, which they enjoyed almost as much. She cleaned the house and washed their clothes. At night, she tucked the boys in and told them a story. Wendy was very strict about bedtime. All the boys had to be in bed by seven in the evening.

After the boys had gone to sleep, she sewed new things for them. She patched the knees in their pants and darned their socks. It was a very busy life for Wendy. She loved to be needed, and she loved her underground life with the boys. The only thing that bothered her was that Tinker Bell did not approve of her.

Tinker Bell lived in the underground house too. She had her own special spot in a nook in the wall. No larger than a birdcage, this was Tinker Bell’s own private place. Unlike the messy boys, Tink was very neat and clean. She didn’t need a mother to take care of her.

No girl, large or small, had a lovelier bedroom than Tinker Bell. Each season, she changed her bedspread to match the colors of the trees and flowers. Her curtains were made of the finest butterfly wings. She always drew her tiny curtains when she was dressing or undressing.

Everyone was very happy to have Wendy around, but not Tinker Bell. Sometimes the fairy kept her anger to herself. Other times Tinker Bell plotted against Wendy. One night Tinker Bell tried, with the help of some fairy friends, to float the sleeping Wendy on a great big leaf back to the mainland. Fortunately, the leaf gave way and Wendy woke up just in time. She fell into the water and swam back.

As time went by, Wendy and her brothers began to forget about the life they had left. Their house in London, their parents, and Nana all seemed very far away. Wendy knew that the nursery window would always be open for her and her brothers to return. What worried her, though, was that John only dimly remembered their parents. And Michael hardly remembered them at all. In fact, Michael thought of Wendy as his mother now.

Wendy felt it was her duty to keep their old life from fading away. She decided to make a test for her brothers—just like in school. The Lost Boys joined in as well. They all made small writing slates for themselves and sat around the table. They began writing and answering the test questions.

Wendy created some "yes or no" questions, such as "Was Father taller than Mother?" She made up multiple choice questions like "What was the color of Mother’s eyes: blue, green, or brown?" She also had them write essays. The topics were "How I Spent my Last Vacation in England" and "A Detailed Description of the Nursery."

Once the boys were finished, Wendy marked their little slates with a check mark if the answers were correct. She’d make an X if they were wrong. Needless to say, the answers the Lost Boys wrote were silly. They had never met Mother and Father or lived in the family’s house in London. Still, they all had fun. Only it was sad to see how many X ’s John had on his test.

Peter was the only boy who did not take the test. Except for Wendy, he hated all mothers. Peter was also the only boy on the island who couldn’t write or spell. He felt he had more important things to think about—like his next adventure.

And adventures occurred every day. Sometimes it was a bear hunt. Other times it was a tangle with the pirates or the Indians. The little underground house was the quiet part of the children’s life. The adventures outside were much livelier. And though Wendy liked their quiet life at home, she admired the daring and carefree spirit of Peter and his gang. John and Michael both enjoyed the excitement of Neverland. But sometimes it was scary and dangerous.

To please Wendy, Peter invented his own game. He would pretend not to have adventures. He pretended to live the life that John and Michael had had before coming to Neverland. He would catch a ball in the air or throw a ball to the other boys. Then they would push each other around, trying to get the ball away from each other.

Peter also went for quiet walks, for what he called a "breath of air." Sometimes he just sat still, watching the sun go down. It was always an unusual sight to see Peter doing nothing. He looked so solemn during these times that one had to laugh. But this game did not last too long. Pretty soon Peter lost interest in pretending to be a normal boy and went back to his adventures.

When Peter went out alone, Wendy never knew quite what to expect. Often he’d say he had just gone out for a "breath of air." But, when Wendy went outside later, she would find something strange on the ground—a torn jacket with golden sleeves or an Indian war club. Other times, he would tell a story about how he shot a grizzly bear. But no bear was ever found. Sometimes he came home from his quiet walk with his head bleeding. Then Wendy would fuss over him and wash his cut with warm water.
She was never quite sure what to believe. But there were some adventures that she knew to be true, because she was in them!

The children spent many sunny days at the lagoon. This was where the mermaids lived and played. Wendy was fascinated by the mermaids and wanted to meet them. But the only human they would talk to was Peter. Sometimes they even let him sit on their tails. When they saw Wendy, however, they would dive back into the water. Then they would use their tails to splash her. So Wendy had to watch from a distance.

The best time to see mermaids was on sunny days after a rain. Then they surfaced in large numbers to play with their bubbles. The bubbles were made of rainbow water. The mermaids hit the colorful bubbles from one to another with their fins until the bubbles burst. It was lovely to watch.

Sometimes the children came to the lagoon. They would sit on Marooners’ Rock to have a picnic lunch. First, they would eat, and then Wendy would insist they rest for half an hour before swimming. Obediently, they would lie down on the rock in the sunlight. Watching over the children, Wendy would gaze at them with great pride.

It was just such a day on Marooners’ Rock when a great adventure occurred. They had all dozed off except for Wendy, who continued to sew. Suddenly a great change came over the lagoon. The sun disappeared, and a chilly breeze made stiff waves in the water. The surface of the rock became cold. Something frightening was coming.

When Wendy saw the dark gloom rising, she should have awakened the boys. But being a new mother, she didn’t know this. Instead, she thought it was more important to stick to her rule of a half hour’s rest. Even when she heard the sound of oncoming oars, she let the boys sleep on. They all continued to sleep—except for Peter. When he heard the splash of oars, he sprang up with excitement.
"Pirates coming—dive!" he yelled. Instantly, the children all dove into the water. The boys and Wendy swam quickly away.

By the time the small pirate boat drew near, Marooners’ Rock was deserted. Three figures stood up in the boat—the pirates Smee and Starkey, and Tiger Lily. The hands and feet of the Indian princess were tied with rope. The pirates’ plan was to leave their captive on Marooners’ Rock. For centuries, evil captains had tied sailors to the rock, waiting for the tide to rise. When the water rose, the men drowned. This was the fate the pirates planned for Tiger Lily too.
Traveling in what was now almost darkness, the pirates crashed into the rock.
"Lift the girl onto the rock!" Smee yelled. The proud Indian maiden did not resist but continued to hold her head high.

Nearby, two heads bobbed up and down in the water. It was Peter and Wendy. Wendy wept at the sight of poor Tiger Lily. Peter was angered by the unfairness of two against one. Even though Tiger Lily had been an enemy of the boys, he now wanted to save her.
Imitating the voice of Hook to perfection, Peter called out, "Ahoy, you pirates!"
"It’s Captain Hook," the pirates said to each other with surprise. "Captain, we have the Indian princess," they shouted.
"Cut her ropes and set her free," commanded Peter in Captain Hook’s voice.
"But Captain . . ." they called back.
"I said set her free at once or you’ll tangle with my hook!" yelled Peter.
"We’d better do what the captain orders," said Smee to Starkey. They cut the ropes on Tiger Lily’s hands and feet. Immediately, she slipped gracefully into the water and swam away from sight.

For a brief moment, there was complete silence in the lagoon. Wendy looked at Peter with great admiration. Peter tried really hard not to look pleased. The pirates struggled to get their boat off the rock.
Suddenly a voice cried out, "Ahoy, you pirates!" It was the voice of the real Captain Hook, and he was in the water too!
Hook swam toward the pirate boat in the growing darkness. Starkey held out the lantern to guide him. Meanwhile, Wendy and Peter were still in the water listening closely to what was happening.
Hook reached the boat and climbed on board.
"Captain, is everything okay?" Smee asked timidly. All Hook could do was let out a sigh. "What’s up, Captain?" Smee asked again.
Finally the captain spoke. "The game is over. Those boys have found a mother to help them." He sighed again.
Wendy felt very proud.
"Oh, what an evil day!" cried Starkey.
"How dreadful! But what’s a mother?" asked Smee.
Wendy was so shocked that she gave out a little yell. Peter had to pull her under the water to keep her quiet.
Hook heard the noise and said, "What’s that?"
"Nothing but the birds," answered Starkey, raising the lantern. They could see a nest floating on the lagoon. A big bird sat on top of it.

"See?" said Hook to Smee, pointing to the bird. "That is a mother. That nest has fallen into the water. But does the mother desert her eggs? No! She will sit on them until they hatch. Then they will become her children. She protects them from all dangers, like falling into the water or being eaten up by fish."
Hook’s description made the pirates wipe tears from their eyes. As they watched the mother bird protecting her young, Smee suddenly had an idea.
"Captain," said Smee, "maybe we could kidnap the Lost Boys’ new mother and make her our mother instead."
"What a great idea!" cried Hook. "We will seize the children and carry them to our ship. We will make the boys walk the plank. Then the girl will become our mother!"
"Never!" cried Wendy. Peter had to push her under the water again.
"What was that?" said Hook, trying to listen in the dark. But everything was quiet now. Then the captain and his pirates shook hands and hook. They all swore to the plan.
"Yes, a girl and a mother is just what we need," said Smee, as if he knew all about mothers now.
Suddenly, Captain Hook remembered another girl—Tiger Lily. "Where is the Indian princess?" he demanded.
"We let her go, just like you told us," said Starkey.
"You let her go?" screamed Hook.
"It was your order. You told us to let her go," said Smee.
"That’s ridiculous! I gave no such order."
Realizing his pirates had been tricked, Hook turned back to the voice he had heard in the dark lagoon. He yelled out, "Do you hear me?"
Though he knew he shouldn’t answer, Peter couldn’t stop himself. "I hear you!" he called back, imitating Hook’s voice once again.
"Who are you, stranger?" Hook demanded.
Peter yelled back, "I am Captain James Hook of the Jolly Roger ."
"You are not!" exclaimed Hook. "If you are Hook, who am I?"
"A codfish!" replied the voice.
"A codfish?" said Hook, confused.
Smee and Starkey drew back from their captain. "Our captain is a codfish? How embarrassing," they said.
Humiliated, Captain Hook decided to challenge the voice. "Have you got another name?" he called.
Peter could never resist a good game, so he answered, "Yes, I have."
"Is it vegetable?" asked Hook.
"No," Peter answered.
"Mineral?"
"No."
"Animal?"
"Yes."
"A man?" asked Hook.
"Certainly not!" cried Peter, annoyed.
"A boy?"
"Yes, yes."
"An ordinary boy?"
"No! A very special boy," answered Peter, losing himself in the fun of the game.
"Hmm," said Hook, pretending to be puzzled.
"Can’t you guess?" cried Peter. "Or do you give up?"
"Yes," said Hook eagerly. "I give up."
"I’m Peter Pan!" shouted Peter with great pride.
"Now we have him!" Hook cried gleefully. "Into the water, Smee and Starkey. Take him, dead or alive."
Hook leapt back into the water.
"Are you ready for battle, my boys?" shouted Peter with great excitement.
From various parts of the lagoon, the boys answered, "Ay, ay! We’ll get those pirates!"

And the battle was on. The boys fought bravely against Smee and Starkey, forcing them out of their boat and into the water. Heads bobbed up and down. It was a close fight. At last, the boys captured the boat, and the two pirates swam away.

Fearless as they were, none of the boys wanted to fight Captain Hook, who was in the water too. They had promised Peter that Captain Hook would be his, but they also trembled at the thought of Hook’s iron claw. It was at this battle, on Marooners’ Rock, that Peter and Hook would finally meet face-to-face!

Hook pulled himself up on the rock to take a breath. Peter climbed up the other side. Because the rock was slippery, they had to crawl on their knees, keeping their heads down. Neither knew the other was coming. As they both reached for a grip on the slippery rock, their hands suddenly touched. Their heads popped up, and Hook and Peter were nose to nose.
Quickly, Peter grabbed the knife from Hook’s belt. But before he struck his foe, Peter noticed that he was on the highest part of the rock. It seemed very unfair.
So instead of stabbing Hook right away, Peter extended his hand to help Hook up so they would both be on equal footing. But rather than taking Peter’s hand, Hook bit it.
Outraged, Peter stood motionless. He was in shock.

People remember the first time life is unfair to them. Though they may forgive the unfairness, they are never quite the same after. But not Peter. He had met unfairness before, but he always forgot. Perhaps this was the real difference between Peter and other boys who grow older. While Peter stood there stunned, Hook’s iron hand clawed him several times. Peter was badly wounded.

During the battle, the Lost Boys lost track of Wendy and Peter. After a while they saw Hook in the water swimming away as fast as he could. Behind him was the crocodile in pursuit of his favorite food. The boys decided to make their way back home. Occasionally they shouted "Peter! Wendy!" but they expected no answer. They were sure that Peter and Wendy had already made it back home.

Left behind, Wendy had swum around the lagoon on her own and was now worn-out. With his last bit of strength, Peter pulled her up onto Marooners’ Rock. They both lay there, tired and weak and unable to speak. The tide was coming in. Finally Peter said, "Look, the water is rising."
Wendy did not understand, so Peter tried to explain. "You’re too weak to swim or fly home, and I am badly wounded. Soon the water will cover this rock."
"You mean we are going to drown?" she asked weakly.
"Unless we find a way to leave this rock," he answered.

As they clung to each other, Peter searched the water for something that might keep them afloat. Floating by was Starkey’s hat. Quickly, Peter grabbed it. But it was too small to be of much help. Nevertheless, he placed it on his head.
Then suddenly something very light brushed against Peter. It was the tail of a kite that was flying high above. Michael had made it some days ago, and it had blown away.
"Look it’s Michael’s kite!" said Peter. "It might be able to carry you home." Peter grabbed hold of it. With new energy, he tied the string of the kite around Wendy’s waist.
"What about you?" asked Wendy. "You must tie it around yourself too."
"This kite isn’t big enough. It will only lift one person," replied Peter.
"I won’t go without you," said Wendy. But, with his last bit of strength, Peter had already pushed her from the rock. In seconds, she was in the air and almost out of sight.

The water kept rising, and Peter was alone in the lagoon on Marooners’ Rock. All he could hear were the mermaids calling good-bye to the moon as they swam to their bedrooms in the sea. Soon the water completely covered the rock and rose above Peter’s ankles. As he waited for his doom, Peter watched the only thing moving on the water. At first he thought it might be a piece of paper, a part of the kite. But then he noticed it was fighting the current and getting closer. Suddenly, he realized it was a bird, and it was trying to reach him.

The bird was still sitting on her nest, but she was guiding it using her wings as paddles. By the time she reached Peter, she was very tired. She was prepared to share her nest with him, even though her eggs were still in it. Her motherly instincts told her that Peter was only a child, and she wanted to save him. The bird called out to Peter and he called out to her. But they couldn’t understand each other’s language.
"I want you to swim to my nest," she called in her language. "I am too tired to bring it any nearer."
"What are you quacking about?" asked Peter.
"I want you to swim to me," called the bird, as clearly as she could.
Peter spoke slowly, thinking that would help. "What . . . are . . . you . . . quacking . . . about?" he called back.
"You silly boy! Why don’t you listen to me?" said the annoyed bird.
Both were exhausted and close to losing their tempers.
But the bird meant to save Peter if she could. With one last try, she pushed the nest against the rock. Then she flew up, circling overhead.
"Oh, now I understand what you’re trying to do!" Peter exclaimed.
He grabbed the nest and waved his thanks to the bird. She waited to see what he would do with her eggs.

Peter pulled out the two large white eggs. Then he remembered Starkey’s hat, which was still on his head. Yes, the hat was watertight. With its wide brim, the hat would easily float on the water. Carefully, he placed the eggs in it and put the hat in the water. It stayed afloat. Peter then got into the nest and took off his shirt to make a sail.

The bird saw what Peter had done and immediately went after the hat. Happy to have her eggs back, she sat down on them to keep them warm. Then she drifted in one direction as Peter drifted in the other. She cried at him and he crowed at her—in shared respect.

When Peter landed near home, he put the nest where the bird could easily find it again. But the bird never came back for it. She was perfectly happy with the hat for her eggs. The broad brim was just right for the young chicks when they finally hatched. It provided an excellent springboard for them while they were learning to fly. And when the hat finally fell apart with age, the bird built her new nests in the shape of a hat ever after.

When Peter finally reached the underground house, everyone was happy. After being carried here and there by the kite, Wendy had also just arrived home. Every boy had his own tale of adventure, and they all spoke at once—except for the twins. But the biggest topic of conversation was that they were already many hours late for bed.

"To bed, to bed, boys!" Wendy cried, and they all went off to bed. The next day, she gave out bandages to everyone, so they could all put their arms into slings. As everyone knows, one cannot win in battle without some serious injuries.

Because of the lagoon adventure, the Indians became Peter’s friends. Peter had saved Tiger Lily’s life. Now she and her tribe kept faithful watch over the Lost Boys’ underground home. Night and day, they guarded Peter and his family. They called Peter "The Great White Father," which he quite liked. He would say to them, "The Great White Father is glad to see the warriors protecting his home from the pirates." But Tiger Lily did not want Wendy to be called Peter’s wife. The Indian princess had become quite fond of the little boy as well. And, like Tinker Bell, she was jealous of Wendy.

One evening, the Indians were at their watch as usual while the children were having dinner below. Peter wasn’t home because he had gone to find out the time. On the island, one found out the time by finding the crocodile. When the clock inside the crocodile struck the hour, one knew what time it was.
The meal was make-believe, and the boys were particularly noisy and difficult. Wendy asked for silence.
"If you have any complaints," she said, "you must first raise your hands to speak." All their hands went up at once.
"Slightly is eating all the food!"
"Nibs is sneezing on the table!"
"The twins took too much dessert!"
"Curly isn’t using his knife and fork!"

After the meal, things quieted down. They all helped clean the table and put the door away. Wendy went back to her sewing while the boys danced and played by the fire. It was a familiar scene in their home, perhaps for the last time.
Suddenly they could hear footsteps above them. "Children, that must be your father," said Wendy. "He likes it when you greet him."

Outside, Peter was saying good night to the Indians. "Keep a safe watch over us tonight!" he said, before slipping into his tree. When he opened the round door underground, the children joyfully dragged him from his tunnel. Peter had brought nuts for the boys and the time of day for Wendy.
"Peter, you will spoil them, you know," Wendy said.
"Father," said Curly, "we’re dancing and we want you to dance with us."
Peter liked dancing, but for fun he pretended to be a tired father coming home from work. "Me?" he groaned. "My old bones can hardly walk!"
"And we want Mother to dance too," said Slightly.
"What?" cried Wendy, joining the game. "This old mother of so many boys has lots to do!"

"But it’s Saturday night!" shouted Michael. However, no one knew if it was really Saturday night. They had lost count of the days of the week long ago. When they wanted to have a special evening, they always called it "Saturday night."

Peter and Wendy promised to dance with them, but first the boys would have to put on their pajamas and get ready for bed. While they waited for the boys, Peter joined Wendy at the fire. She looked at him lovingly.
"They are sweet, our little family, don’t you think?" said Wendy. Peter suddenly looked troubled. "What is it, Peter?"
"It’s only make-believe that I am their father, right?" replied Peter in a shaky voice.
"Oh, yes," said Wendy.
"You see," he continued, "it would make me old to be their real father."
"Peter, after all this time together, what do I mean to you?" asked Wendy.
His answer was not what she had hoped for. "I am your devoted son," replied Peter.
"I understand," she said, but it really was very confusing. Wendy got up from her seat and went to another corner of the room.
"Sometimes you are very strange," Peter said to her. "And so is Tiger Lily. She says she wants to mean something to me, but doesn’t want to be my mother."
"Perhaps Tinker Bell can explain it to you," Wendy answered, frowning.

When the boys returned in their pajamas, they all sang and danced. Soon their dancing turned into a noisy pillow fight. Wendy quieted them and told them it was time for a good-night story. She would tell them the story they loved best, but it was a story that Peter hated. Usually when she told this story, Peter would put his hands over his ears or leave the room. But tonight he remained on his stool. This story was closest to Wendy’s heart, and it began like this: "Once upon a time, there was a man called Mr. Darling and he lived with a woman called Mrs. Darling."
"I knew them," John interrupted.
"I think I knew them too," Michael joined in.

"They lived in a big house in London," Wendy continued, "and had three darling children. The children had a faithful nanny called Nana. But one evening, Mr. Darling was angry with Nana and chained her up in the yard. So the three children flew away."
"This is a really good story," said Nibs.
"They flew away to Neverland where the lost children live," continued Wendy.
"That’s us!" cried the Lost Boys, excited.
"And was one of the lost children called Tootles?" asked Tootles, who already knew the story well.
"Yes," replied Wendy. "But the parents were very sad that their children had flown away. And they visited the nursery every night waiting for their children to return."
"This is a sad story. I don’t see how it can have a happy ending," said Nibs, forgetting what followed.

"Don’t worry," said Wendy. "It turns out all right at the end because the children knew their mother would always leave the window open for them to fly back home. Mothers are loyal like that. And because the children knew this, they stayed away for a long time and had fun."
"Did they ever go back home to their parents?" asked the boys.
This was the part of the story that Peter really hated.

"Yes. One day, they decided to fly back to the open nursery window," Wendy said. "Their mother and father greeted them with much love. They didn’t even scold them for running away. And the whole family lived happily ever after."
That was the story and everyone was very pleased with its ending—except for Peter. He hated grown-ups. He had his own story to tell about mothers.
"Wendy, you are wrong about mothers," he said. And the boys gathered around him to hear his story—one that he had never told before.

"Long ago," he told them, "I thought—like you, Wendy—that my mother would always keep the window open for me. So I stayed away for many moons and suns. Then I flew back, but the window was locked. My mother had forgotten about me. And there was another little boy sleeping in my bed."

This tale scared all the boys, especially John and Michael, who had been listening closely. The Lost Boys had been away from their mothers for a long time and so knew how to live without them. But John and Michael didn’t know how. "Wendy, let’s go home," they both cried.
Wendy put her arms around them and thought about their request for a moment. "Yes," she said. "Maybe it is time to go home to our parents."
The Lost Boys were shocked by this quick decision. "Tonight?" they asked, confused.
"Yes, at once," Wendy replied. Suddenly an image of her mother crying in the empty nursery came to her mind.

Peter, of course, refused to show his feelings to the group. Though he cared very much, he said coolly to Wendy, "If you wish, I’ll make the necessary arrangements." But, in his heart of hearts, he wanted to cry.
Peter slid up his tunnel and went out to make arrangements for Wendy, John, and Michael’s trip home. He gave orders to the Indians to guide Wendy and her brothers through the woods.
Then Peter returned to the underground home, where an unfortunate sight greeted him. Upset that they were going to lose Wendy, the Lost Boys were frantic.
"After you leave, things will be worse than before you came!"
"We won’t let you go."
"We’ll keep you as our prisoner."
"Chain her up!"
They shouted at her.
Only Tootles protected Wendy. He took out his sword and faced the other boys. This wasn’t like the usual Tootles.
He stood up tall and straight and proud. "I will strike the first one who does not behave well toward Wendy," he said bravely. The other boys backed off.
Then they noticed Peter. They saw that he would not support them either.

"I would never," said Peter, "keep a girl in Neverland against her will. I’ve asked the Indians to guide you through the woods," he explained to Wendy. "Then Tinker Bell will take you across the sea. Wake Tinker Bell up, Nibs."

Nibs knocked twice on the wall beside Tinker Bell’s nook. Her curtains were drawn, but of course she had been listening all along. The fairy was delighted that Wendy was leaving, but she did not want to be her guide. Without opening her curtains, she refused.
"Tink says she won’t go!" Nibs yelled. He was surprised that she dared to disobey Peter.
Peter went directly to Tinker Bell himself. "Tink," he demanded, "if you don’t get up and dress at once, I will open your curtains. Then we will see you in your nightgown."
This made the vain fairy leap to the floor. "Who said I wasn’t getting up?" she cried.
Meanwhile, Wendy, John, and Michael were getting ready for their journey. The Lost Boys watched, growing sadder and sadder at the thought of Wendy leaving.

When they began to cry, Wendy softly said, "Dear boys, if you want to come with me, I’m sure my mother and father will adopt you." This invitation was actually meant for Peter, but she offered it to the rest of the boys out of kindness.
"Peter, can we go with Wendy?" they asked.
"All right," he said with a bitter smile. They went to pack their knapsacks for the trip. Wendy and the boys both thought Peter would be joining them. But Peter, of course, had no intention of going.
"Get your things, Peter," said Wendy.
"No," he answered, pretending not to care. "I’m not going with you." Then to show that none of this mattered to him, he skipped around the room playing his flute.
"Don’t you want to find your mother?" Wendy asked. She didn’t want to leave him behind.
"Even if I had one, I hardly remember her," said Peter. "Anyway, she would just force me to grow up. And I want to stay a little boy and have fun."
When Wendy told the boys that Peter wasn’t coming, they wondered if he would let them go without him.
"Let’s not make a fuss," said Peter, too proud to show his feelings. "Good-bye, boys. Good-bye, Wendy." He held out his hand to her. She took it sadly, but wished he had hugged or kissed her instead.
"Please remember to eat properly, Peter," she said, almost crying. "And don’t forget to take your medicine. I’ve put it in a cup for you."
A sad moment followed. The sadness made Peter uncomfortable, so he interrupted the silence. "Are you ready, Tink?" he called out. "Lead the way."
Tinker Bell darted up the nearest tunnel to the outside world.
But before anyone could follow her, the sound of a brutal battle erupted above. At that very moment, the pirates had attacked the Indians on top of the Lost Boys’ home.

The battle above was so loud, the earth seemed to move. The children heard screams of terror and Indian war cries. Stunned, they stopped packing for their trip and opened their mouths in alarm. They fell silent as stones, listening for a clue to how the battle was going.

For the Indians, however, the attack was not a complete surprise. From the moment the pirates had landed on the island, and one had stepped on a dry stick, the Indians had known the pirates were there and expected a fight. They had even sent scouts out to investigate. But the Indians were used to sneaking up on an enemy camp at dawn. Everyone knew this was how battles with Indians were supposed to go. So the Indians waited, expecting the pirates to stop and set up camp.

The cunning Captain Hook fooled them. It was the pirates who snuck up on the Indians, and they attacked late in the night. Surprised, the Indian warriors grabbed their weapons and yelled out their war cries. They had promised to guard the children’s home, and they fought bravely to the end. But they were beaten. Only Tiger Lily and a few Indian warriors survived the battle. And they quickly fled.
Hook watched the pirates wipe their swords and catch their breath. "Well done, men," he grinned. "But the night’s work is not over yet."
"What? What does he mean?" said the pirates to one another.
"You see," Hook went on, "The Indians aren’t really who I was after. I want to capture Wendy and the Lost Boys. And most of all, I want the blood of Peter Pan!"

Peter was such a little boy that it is hard to imagine why Hook hated him so much. True, Peter had cut off Hook’s hand and thrown it to the crocodile. But it was Peter’s pride that really made Hook’s blood boil.
"How can a boy so young be so boastful?" he wondered. Just thinking about it made his iron claw twitch.

The question now for Hook was how to get the pirates down into Peter’s underground home. He knew his pirates were too big to fit into the small boys’ hollow trees. And they would never squeeze through the tunnels to the underground home.
Hook looked over at his men and said quietly, "Now which of you is the skinniest?"
Down below, Peter, Wendy, and the boys were anxious.
"The noise has finally stopped," Peter said. "The battle must be over."
"Yes, but which side has won?" asked Wendy, worried. Their lives depended on the answer.
"If the Indians have won," answered Peter, "they will beat their drum. It is their victory signal. So we must listen." At this, Wendy and the children all went silent again.
Meanwhile, looking for a place to rest, Smee found the Indians’ drum and sat on it. "No one will hear this drum again," he said to himself, pleased.

But to his surprise, Hook whispered, "Smee, beat the drum." Captain Hook was just as clever as Peter, and Smee smiled when he understood what his sneaky captain was up to. Smee beat the drum, and the sound rang through the woods.

Below ground the boys yelled, "It’s an Indian victory!" They let out a cheer so loud that the pirates heard it above. The boys repeated their good-byes to Peter and prepared to come up through the hollow trees.

Above them the pirates smiled evilly at each other and rubbed their hands. Hook silently motioned each pirate to pick a hollow tree and watch it. In this way, they would catch the boys as they emerged from the ground.
The first to come out of his tree was Curly—right into the arms of Cecco.

"Here, catch!" yelled Cecco as he threw Curly to Smee. Smee threw him to Starkey, who threw him to the next pirate in line, until he landed at the feet of Captain Hook. Each boy was captured this way and tossed around like a sack of potatoes. But Wendy was treated differently. When she came out, Hook raised his hat to her with unusual respect. He offered her his arm and guided her to the spot where the others were being gagged. Not knowing what else to do, Wendy took his arm. She was only a frightened little girl, after all. Now the only one left below was Peter.
To prevent Wendy and the boys from flying away, Hook had cut a long rope into nine equal pieces.

"Tie up these boys, and tie them up tight!" ordered Hook. The pirates tied up each captive in turn. This went smoothly until they got to Slightly. The pirates struggled to get the rope around his plump body.

"This piece of rope must be shorter than the rest," said Cecco angrily. But the truth was, Slightly had become quite fat from eating Wendy’s cooking. In fact, as he had gained weight, he had found it more and more difficult to fit through his tree tunnel. So Slightly had been carving out the inside of his tree trunk. As his belly swelled, his tunnel had gotten larger and larger—until it was now wide enough for a grown-up man.
Seeing his pirates struggling to tie Slightly, the clever Captain Hook guessed what the boy had done. But he told no one what he had discovered.
"Take these captives to the ship," he commanded his men.
