Alone at last, Hook tiptoed to Slightly’s tree. He put his ear to the opening, but could hear nothing from below. At the bottom of Slightly’s tunnel was the unknown land of Hook’s enemy. Was Peter asleep? Or was he waiting, dagger in hand? A brave man, Hook held his breath and slid down the tree.
Unaware of what had happened above, Peter had pretended to be carefree when Wendy and the boys had left.

"I think I’ll play my flute," he said, and for a while he did. Then he decided not to take his medicine, just to upset Wendy. He put the cup filled with medicine back on the shelf. Then Peter lay down across the great bed on top of the covers. He knew this would annoy Wendy, who liked to tuck the boys under the covers.

Peter started to cry, but then he realized how hurt Wendy would be if he laughed instead. So he started to laugh and fell fast asleep. One of his arms dropped over the edge of the bed. Both legs were relaxed and spread out. And the unfinished part of his laugh was still on his mouth.
It was in this helpless pose that Hook found Peter when he slid out the bottom end of the tunnel.

Hook stood silent in the underground room. He watched his enemy asleep on the bed. How could he kill Peter at this moment? It was not that Hook felt pity for Peter, but rather that he had never imagined killing his enemy so easily. Hook had expected a ferocious battle with swords flashing. At the end of the battle, Hook would kill Peter and stand tall, the proud winner. But seeing his enemy asleep and defenseless took all the glory out of the imagined fight. Then Hook noticed the little grin on Peter’s face. It reminded the pirate that he was deeply irritated by Peter’s pride and arrogant confidence. He could not let this chance to kill Peter go by! Looking about, Hook saw a medicine cup on a shelf. Suddenly he had a wonderful and evil idea. He would poison Peter.

Captain Hook always carried a bottle of poison in his pocket to make sure he could never be captured alive. He had made the poison himself, so he knew it was effective. Hook added five drops to Peter’s medicine and rubbed his hook against his hand with excitement. Then, with a triumphant look at his victim, he slid his way back up and out of the tree.

Peter slept on. He knew nothing about the massacre of his Indian friends or about the capture of Wendy and the boys. He didn’t know about Hook coming into his home or about the dangerous cup of medicine standing on the shelf.
Finally he was awakened by a soft, careful knock on the door of his tunnel. Peter grabbed his dagger and shouted, "Who is it?"
"Let me in quickly, Peter!" said Tinker Bell in her bell-like voice.
Peter opened the round door and she flew into the room. Her little face was flushed and her dress stained with mud.
"What is it, Tink?" asked Peter.
"Oh, you could never guess!" she cried. Then she told him the terrible news about how Wendy and the boys had been captured.

As Peter listened, his heart beat faster and faster. Wendy was tied up and on the pirate ship? He had to rescue her! Already he had forgotten how angry he was with her. Wanting to please her, he went to get the medicine off the shelf.
"Don’t do that!" screamed Tinker Bell. She had heard Hook muttering as he went through the forest, and she had learned about the poison.
"Why not?" asked Peter.
"Your medicine is poisoned. Hook did it while you slept," she said.
"Don’t be silly," Peter said. "You know that no grown-up can enter here."
Tinker Bell could not explain how Hook had done it because she didn’t know the secret of Slightly’s tree.
"Besides," said Peter, not wanting to admit that he had cried and fallen asleep, "I never fell asleep."
He raised the cup to his lips. Like a bolt of lightning, Tinker Bell flew between his lips and the liquid. She drank the whole cup.
"How dare you drink my medicine!" he yelled.
But Tinker Bell did not answer. Already she was fluttering dizzily in the air.
"What’s the matter with you?" asked Peter, suddenly afraid.
"I told you," she said softly. "It was poisoned, and now I'm going to die."
"Oh, Tink, you drank the poison to save my life," he said. "Why did you do it?"
"Don’t be silly, Peter," she whispered. "You know why." Tinker Bell flew slowly to her nook and lay on her bed. As Peter watched, her light grew fainter and fainter.
For the second time in just a few hours, Peter began to cry. Tink’s voice, now very low, stopped his tears for a moment.
"If enough children believe in fairies," she told him, "I know I will get well again."

There were no children left in the house, but Peter knew what he could do. He called out to all the children who might be dreaming. Peter knew that in their dreams children were nearer to Neverland than anyone imagined.
"Do you believe?" he shouted. "If you do, please clap your hands!" Never before had Peter said "please" in such a sincere way. He stretched out his arms and cried, "Don’t let Tinker Bell die!"

Suddenly there was a roar of clapping from around the world. And as parents all over rushed to their children’s rooms to see what was the matter, Tinker Bell sat up in bed. Her light was bright once again. Peter had saved her!

It was a dark, starless night. The moon was hidden in the cloudy sky. Peter crawled on his belly, snakelike, across the ground. This was one of many useful things the Indians had taught him. Tinker Bell was still too weak to fly and light the way, so Peter had decided not to fly himself. He knew where he was headed—the pirate ship, the Jolly Roger !

Suddenly, Peter caught sight of the crocodile, which was also creeping in the dark. No other living creature seemed to be awake but the boy and the crocodile. And they were both after the same prey—Captain Hook. In the silence of the night, Peter realized something was different about the crocodile. The clock inside it had finally stopped ticking. At that moment, Peter had an idea. He was determined to rescue Wendy and the boys, but he was also eager to destroy his rival.
"This time, it’s Hook or me!" he thought with great excitement. And he started to form a plan.

The Jolly Roger was anchored not far from the shore of Kidd’s Creek. On board, some of the pirates were sleeping, and others were playing dice and cards. Even though it was after midnight, Smee sat at the ship’s sewing machine, busily mending the captain’s clothes. Hook walked the deck deep in thought. This should have been his moment of triumph. Peter was dead. The boys were tied up and soon would walk the plank. And Wendy was his captive. But Hook felt unhappy and alone.

Even among his pirates, Hook was lonely. They were no better than dogs that obeyed him. They certainly were not equals who could listen to his feelings. How cruel fate had been to the captain! Hook hadn’t always been a pirate. Hook wasn’t even his real name. Once, he had been a promising young man at a private school. There he had learned the manners and fancy dress that could have made him a gentleman. But he had wanted fame, and evil had taken hold of him.
"What good are all my evil triumphs in the end? No little children love me," he thought.

It was strange that he should suddenly think of these things. Maybe it was the sound of Smee’s sewing machine. Even though he was a pirate, old Smee was lovable. There was not a child on board the ship who did not already love Smee. He had given Wendy a cloak to keep warm, and Michael had even tried on his glasses.
"What does Smee have that I do not?" wondered Hook.
He needed to do something wicked to feel better again. Standing a little taller, Hook shouted to his men, "Are all the boys chained so they cannot fly away?"
"Ay, ay," they answered.

"Then bring them up," he ordered. The poor prisoners were dragged from the hold below. The eight boys stood in a line in front of him. "Six of you will walk the plank tonight. But I will keep two to be my cabin boys. Who wishes to serve me?"
The boys were silent. Finally Tootles spoke up. "Sir, I don’t think my mother would like me to be a pirate. Would your mother like you to be a pirate, Slightly?"
"I don’t think so," Slightly answered sadly, as if he wished it were otherwise. The other boys agreed.
Hook was angry. He looked directly at John. "You seem to have a little more courage, boy," he said. "Did you ever want to be a pirate?"
John became thoughtful. "Yes, there was a time when I wanted to be a pirate." Then he looked around at his friends. "But that was long ago."
"Then go to your doom!" Hook roared. To his men he said, "Get the plank ready! And bring up their mother to watch!"

Wendy was brought up to the deck of the Jolly Roger . The boys were lined up in their chains trying to look brave. When she saw the pirates preparing the plank, she was filled with hate. She hated Hook and she hated the pirates. Boys might think pirates exciting, but Wendy did not. She especially hated that the ship had not been cleaned for years. Not one window was without a layer of grime. In fact, while she was below, she wrote "Dirty Pig" on a window with her finger. She also hated that it was nighttime and no one was in bed. But when the boys gathered around her, all these thoughts melted away.
"So, my beauty," said Hook, "soon you will see your children walk the plank." Hook’s lace collar was dirty, and when he saw Wendy staring, he tried to hide it.
"Are the children going to die?" she asked scornfully. Her voice made it clear how she despised Hook for his plan.
"They are!" he shouted. "Silence! Listen to a mother’s last words to her children."
Wendy stood tall and faced everyone proudly. "These are my last words, dear boys," she said. "I feel that your real mothers would say this: We hope our sons die like gentlemen."
Hook shuddered. Even the pirates were awed, for Wendy’s words were the kind that inspired bravery.
Tootles cried out, "I am going to do what my mother wishes. What are you going to do, Slightly?"
"What my mother wishes," said Slightly. "What are you going to do, Nibs?"
Nibs answered the same way, and so did the other boys until Hook interrupted.
"Tie her up to the mast!" he shouted cruelly.
It was Smee who tied Wendy. Under his breath, he whispered, "I’ll save you if you promise to be my mother." But this was a promise Wendy could never make to a pirate.

The boys’ eyes had drifted from Wendy to the plank, and their faces went white. They were not ready to die. Their walk down the narrow board and over the end into the cold sea would be the last walk they would ever take. They shivered and stared, no longer sure they could walk the plank as gentlemen. They were, after all, only little boys.

Hook smiled and took a step toward Wendy. He wanted to turn her face to make her watch the boys walk the plank. He wanted to hear her cries of terror and regret. Instead, what he heard filled his own heart with terror. It was the tick-tock of the crocodile.
They all heard it—Hook, the other pirates, the boys, and Wendy. Instantly, they all looked—but not at the water where the sound was coming from. All their eyes were fixed on Captain Hook.

The crocodile, Hook knew, had only one victim in mind—him! He fell to the floor, trembling in a heap. The ticking grew louder, as if the crocodile were getting closer. Hook crawled on his knees to the other side of the ship, away from the boys and Wendy. The awful sound was getting even louder. All Hook could imagine was the terrible crocodile climbing aboard his ship.
"Hide me!" Hook cried, but his men stepped back to clear the way. They had always been loyal to their captain, but none of them would stand between him and his fate.

On the other side of the deck, the boys leaned over the side of the ship to see the crocodile climb in. But to their surprise, it was not the crocodile coming to their rescue. It was Peter! He made a sign for them to keep silent. Then he went on ticking.

Peter arrived at the shore of Kidd’s Creek where the Jolly Roger was anchored. He had quickly crawled across the island. After seeing the silent crocodile, Peter had decided to imitate it. In fact, he tick-tocked so perfectly the way the creature had done that the other animals let him pass unharmed. The crocodile, which had become fond of the sound, followed him, hoping to get his tick-tock back.

"This time, it’s Hook or me!" Peter vowed to himself, then dived into the water. He had been tick-tocking so long that he hardly thought about it anymore. He swam to the ship and climbed up the side—tick-tocking all the while.

When the boys looked over the side, he signaled them to be quiet. Then he climbed around the hull to the other side of the ship. He peeked over the rail and saw the boys in chains and Wendy tied to the mast. They all saw him too, and he gave them another signal to be quiet. Hook was trembling on the deck.
"How clever of me!" Peter thought, grinning.

At the back of the deck was the cabin. Peter watched the cabin door. When one of the pirates came out, Peter stabbed him with his dagger. He covered the pirate’s mouth to muffle his dying moan. The boys watched as Peter threw the pirate overboard. There was a loud splash, followed by silence. Then Peter vanished into the cabin.
"Pirate number one!" whispered Slightly.
The pirates had heard a big splash, and then the tick-tocking had stopped. All they could hear now was the sound of their breathing.
"It’s gone, Captain," Smee said, wiping his spectacles. "All is still again."

Listening hard, Hook slowly raised his head. Hearing nothing, he got up and yelled, "Get those boys on the plank!" His nerve was back. But the boys had seen him act like a coward, and it made him hate them more. "Fetch my whip from the cabin!" he yelled to one of his pirates.
"The cabin! Peter’s in there!" thought the children, as they looked at each other.

"Ay, ay," said Bill Jukes, cheerfully opening the cabin door. As soon as the door closed behind him, a terrible scream was heard from inside. It was followed by a sound like a rooster crowing. The boys knew the sound, but the pirates looked puzzled.
"Number two!" Slightly said quietly to the boys.
"What was that?" shouted Hook.
Cecco thought for a moment, and then ran into the cabin. Shocked, he stumbled out.
"What’s the matter?" Hook yelled.
"Juke’s been stabbed to death," cried Cecco. "The cabin is dark, and there is some terrible thing in there. It’s . . . crowing."
"Cecco," Hook ordered, "go find out what that thing is!"
"No, no! I can’t do that!" Cecco said, desperately.
Hook lifted his iron claw. "Are you disobeying me?" he yelled.
Trembling, Cecco followed Hook’s order and went slowly into the cabin. Again, they all heard a deadly scream followed by a crowing sound.
"Number three!" Slightly called out.
Hook yelled at his crew. "Who will get this crowing thing?"
"Wait until Cecco comes out," cried Starkey.
The other pirates agreed. "Yes, let’s wait!"
"Did I hear you volunteer, Starkey?" said Hook.
"No, by thunder!" growled Starkey. "I’ll hang before I go in there."
"Is this mutiny?" asked Hook, lifting his claw.
"Captain, please, have mercy!" the fearful pirate begged.

Starkey backed away, and Hook strode toward him, his hook ready to strike. Starkey looked around for help, but all the other pirates were looking down at their feet. With a hopeless scream, Starkey leapt off the ship and into the sea.
"Number four!" called Slightly, happily.
"You cowards!" cried Captain Hook. Grabbing a lantern, he raised his claw. "I’ll bring that thing out here myself." Hook angrily dashed into the cabin.
"Five?" wondered Slightly.
But soon Hook came staggering out without his lantern. "Something blew out my light," he said nervously.
"What about Cecco?" asked Noodler.
"He’s as dead as Bill Jukes," replied Hook.
The pirates were scared, but they saw that Hook was afraid too. They started to make fun of him. The mutiny that Captain Hook had joked about seemed to be really happening.
"Are you scared, Captain Hook?" asked Cookson. "They say that a ship is cursed when a stranger is aboard. Does the crowing thing have crocodile teeth and a tail?"
"Does it have a hook?" asked Robert Mullins. "Is it the devil?"
"This ship is doomed! Let’s mutiny!" cried Skylights.
One by one, all the pirates repeated the cry: "We’re doomed! Mutiny!"
Hearing the pirates, the boys let out a cheer.
But Hook wasn’t beaten yet, and his face lit up with a wicked idea. He looked at the boys.

"My sweet lads," he said, in an evil tone, turning to his pirates. "Open the cabin door and push the prisoners in. Let them fight the crowing thing! If they kill it, wonderful! If it kills them, we are no worse than before."

The brilliance of this plan surprised the other pirates, and they stopped their mutiny. For one last time, they obeyed. Still chained, the boys pretended to struggle but allowed themselves to be pushed into the cabin. With a yell, the pirates closed the cabin door.

"Now let’s listen!" cried Hook. He stepped back and they all turned away. Even though the door was closed, none of the pirates could bear to look at it. They listened, waiting for the screams and the crowing.
Meanwhile Wendy, still bound to the mast, watched. She wasn’t waiting for the screams or the crowing, but for Peter to appear. She knew he had come to save them all.

Inside the cabin, Peter found what he had hoped would be there—the keys to free the boys. After Peter removed their chains, the boys found some weapons and snuck out onto the deck. Hook and the pirates still had their backs turned. The boys hid, while Peter crept to the mast and cut Wendy’s ropes. Now Peter, the boys, and Wendy were free to fly back home. But Peter remembered his vow: "This time, it’s Hook or me!"
Wendy joined the boys in hiding, and Peter took her place at the mast. He put her cloak around him, covered his head, took a deep breath, and crowed loudly.
Hearing this sound, the pirates immediately believed all the boys were dead in the cabin. They were terrified. Seeing the wild look in his men’s eyes, Hook grew afraid they might turn on him again.
"Lads, listen to me," he said, thinking quickly. "It’s the girl! Our bad luck comes from having a girl on board. Everything will be right again when she’s gone."
The men thought for a moment.
"He’s right," Cookson said. "I recall an old saying about girls bringing bad luck."
"Throw the girl overboard!" the pirates cried as they rushed to the mast.
"No one can save you now, missy," Hook hissed to the figure in the cloak.
"There’s one that can save me," the figure replied.
"Who’s that?" Hook said.
"Peter Pan, the avenger!" came the answer. And with those words, Peter flung off the cloak.
"To battle, boys! Attack!" Peter’s voice rang out. In an instant, the boys raised their weapons and charged the pirates.

Swords clashed and screams pierced the air. Stunned, the pirates scattered around the deck, and the boys hunted them down in pairs. Though the pirates were stronger, they were surprised by how fierce the boys were. Separated and alone, each pirate thought he was the last one alive. Some jumped into the sea; others hid in the dark corners of the ship. Tootles, instead of fighting, ran around the deck with a lantern. He shone his light in the faces of hiding pirates, blinding them. Then the other boys took over. Slightly continued to count the victims—five, six, seven, eight, nine. The count grew until they were all dead. Even John and Michael managed to kill a pirate or two.
With his pirates gone, Hook was surrounded by the boys, but he kept them back with his sword and hook.
Then Peter arrived. "Put away your swords, boys," he called. "This man is mine!"
Face to face, the two enemies stared at each other. Hook growled, while Peter smiled.
"So, Peter Pan, this is all your doing," said Hook.
"Yes, and this time, it’s you or I!" Peter challenged.
"Then prepare to die!" cried Hook.

Their weapons flashed and the battle began! Peter was an excellent swordsman, fast and precise. But he was small, and he struggled to get close enough to strike Hook’s chest. Hook, though not quite as quick, was experienced and skilled. But he found it hard to land his blade on his hated foe. Light as a feather, Peter fluttered around, always avoiding Hook’s sword. Then the captain swung at Peter with the point of his hook. But Peter ducked under it, lunged forward, and pierced Hook between the ribs. At the sight of his own blood, Hook dropped his sword.
The boys cried, "Hooray!"

Peter hushed them and invited his foe to pick up his sword. Humiliated by Peter’s display of fairness, Hook was now furious. He no longer cared whether he won or lost. All that mattered was that Peter should die. He rushed to the cannon, known as Long Tom, and hooked a bag of gunpowder with his iron claw. With his good hand, he held up a lantern, threatening to light the powder with its flame.
"We will all be blown to bits!" Hook screamed.

Like an arrow, Peter flew straight at the bag, grabbed it, and threw it overboard. Then he marched toward Hook with his dagger. Hook sprang onto the rail at the side of the ship and threw himself into the water. Sadly, the pirate captain was unaware that the crocodile had followed Peter and was swimming around the ship. That was the last anyone saw of Captain James Hook.
"Hooray!" shouted the boys.
Wendy glowed with pride at Peter’s success. The boys crowded around her, and she praised them all equally. Then she took them into Hook’s cabin and pointed to his watch hanging on a nail.

"It’s one thirty in the morning!" she said. "You should all be asleep!" Quickly she got the children to bed in the pirates’ bunks and tucked them in. There was no time for a story, but they didn’t need one. They only had to remember the grand adventure of that very night.

Only Peter stayed up on the deck of the Jolly Roger . He paced up and down, thinking about Wendy, about her leaving Neverland, and about the trip home. Finally he fell asleep. Wendy found him in the night, curled up beside Long Tom. She bent over and kissed him on the cheek.

The next morning, Peter was the new captain of the Jolly Roger . The boys took their places as crew. They even pretended to be pirates for a while. Peter made a brief speech and everyone cheered. As the wind filled the sails, they headed for England. Captain Peter calculated they would reach the coast in a couple of days. Then they would fly the rest of the way to their final destination—the home of Wendy, John, and Michael.

Wendy, John, and Michael sailed home. As they enjoyed the salty ocean breeze and the rolling waves, they imagined their homecoming at Number 14. They pictured their mother’s delight, their father’s shout of joy, and Nana’s leap to embrace them.

In fact, everything in the nursery was already prepared for them. The beds were made, the window was open, and Mrs. Darling was waiting—just as she had every day since they had left. The only change was that between nine in the morning and six at night Nana’s dog house was not in the nursery.

When the children flew away, Mr. Darling felt that he was to blame. After all, he had chained up Nana and left the children alone. Nana, he realized, had been the wise one. If anyone deserved to be locked up, Mr. Darling decided, it was he. He crawled into Nana’s dog house and wouldn’t allow her in. When Mrs. Darling begged him to come out, he said, "No, dear, this is where I belong." He swore that he would never leave the dog house until his children came back.

Every morning, a taxi came to pick up Mr. Darling in the dog house and took him to his office. In the evening, he came home the same way. Soon the news leaked out to his neighbors. They were saddened by the Darlings’ tragedy and by Mr. Darling’s grief. Crowds would follow his taxi home, touched by his devotion.

On the day of the children’s return, Mrs. Darling was in the nursery waiting for her husband. She was a very sad woman now. She had lost her cheerfulness when she lost her children. The sparkle in the right corner of her mouth, where she kept her secret kiss, had dimmed. Tearfully she said to Nana, "Last night, I dreamed my little ones had come home." Nana put her paw gently on Mrs. Darling's lap. And there they sat until George was brought home in his dog house.

When he arrived home from work, Mr. Darling was carried up to the nursery. He stuck his head out of the dog house to kiss his wife. He sat like that for a while, with his head outside the dog house, talking to Mrs. Darling and holding her hand.

"I am so full of sadness and regret," he sighed. Then he curled up in his dog house for a nap. "Won’t you play me something on the piano to put me to sleep?" he asked. "And shut the nursery window, dear. I feel a chilly draft."
"Oh, George, don’t ever ask me to do that!" said Mrs. Darling. "The window must always be left open for the children."
Mr. Darling apologized, and Mrs. Darling went into the other room to play the piano. Soon he was asleep. And while he slept, Peter and Tinker Bell flew into the nursery.

After defeating the pirates, Peter could have returned to his underground home. He could have stayed there and let Tinker Bell guide Wendy, John, and Michael home—just as he had first planned. But Peter had changed his mind. He sailed on the Jolly Roger because he had come up with a new scheme. He and Tinker Bell arrived ahead of the others to put his scheme into action.

"Quick, Tink," Peter whispered, "close the window! Now you and I must hide by the door. When Wendy flies by, she will think her mother has shut her out forever. Then she will have to go back to Neverland with me."

Peter danced around the nursery with joy, and Tinker Bell followed his every move. They ignored Mr. Darling asleep in Nana’s dog house. Peter peeked into the other room to see who was playing the piano. He whispered to Tink, "That’s Wendy’s mother. She’s a pretty lady, but not as pretty as Wendy."
All of a sudden, the music stopped, and Peter saw that Mrs. Darling was crying. Her heart seemed to be broken.

"She wants me to open the window," thought Peter, "but I won’t!" Peter took a step closer and saw the tears shining on her cheeks. "She’s awfully fond of Wendy," he thought. Then he said stubbornly, "But so am I!"
Mrs. Darling continued to cry, and Peter couldn’t look at her anymore. He skipped about and made funny faces, but this didn’t help. He began to feel sorry for her.
"Oh, all right," he said at last and opened the window. "Come on, Tink," he called. "We don’t want any silly mothers anyway." And he and Tinker Bell flew out the window again.
When Wendy, John, and Michael arrived, they found the window open, just as Mrs. Darling had left it for them. They flew in and looked around. Everything in the nursery looked very familiar.
"I think I’ve been here before," said Michael.
"Of course you have, silly. There is your old bed," said Wendy, pointing.
"So it is," said Michael, as though he really remembered.
"And look," cried John, "there’s Nana’s dog house. Perhaps Nana is in there." He went to look. "There’s a man inside!" he said in a surprised voice.
"It’s Father!" cried Wendy.

"Let me look at him," Michael begged. He took a good look. "He’s not as big as the pirate I killed in Neverland," he said with disappointment. Thankfully, Mr. Darling was still asleep and did not hear him.
"Surely," said John, who had lost faith in his own memory, "Father didn’t always sleep in a dog house."
Just then Mrs. Darling started to play the piano again.
"That must be Mother," cried Wendy.
"Then you’re not really our mother, Wendy?" asked Michael.
Wendy looked at Michael in a wistful way and patted his head.
"Let’s surprise Mother," suggested John. "We’ll put our hands over her eyes and ask her to guess who we are."

Wendy thought they should break the news more gently. "Let’s get into our beds," she suggested. "We’ll be there when she comes in, as if we had never left." The children all ran to their beds and jumped between the sheets, pulling the covers up to their chins.

When Mrs. Darling went back to the nursery to see if her husband was still asleep, all the beds were filled. The children waited for her cry of joy, but it didn’t come. She had dreamed so many times that her children were still in their beds that she thought this was just another dream. As she had often done before, she sat in the chair by the fire and closed her eyes.
The children were disappointed. "Mother!" cried Wendy.
"That’s Wendy," said Mrs. Darling, sure it was her dream.
"Mother!" cried John.
"That’s John," she said.
"Mother!" cried Michael. He knew her now.
"That’s Michael," she said.
Then she opened her eyes. And all three children jumped out of bed and ran into her arms.
"George, George!" she cried, "The children are back!" Mr. Darling woke up in the dog house and Nana came rushing in.
It was a beautiful sight. So beautiful, in fact, that it would have warmed the heart of anyone who looked on. But no one else was watching, no one except for a little boy staring through the window.

While the Darling family was happily hugging upstairs, the Lost Boys were waiting outside. Wendy needed time to tell her parents about them, so the boys counted to five hundred before knocking on the front door. They thought this was more polite than flying through the window.
When Mr. and Mrs. Darling opened the door, the boys stood in a row, looking as innocent as they could. Each had a sweet grin on his face and an eager spark in his eyes.

"We are very pleased to meet you," the boys said together. All their attention was on Mrs. Darling, for they hoped she would be their new mother. Of course she told the boys right away that she would adopt them.
But Mr. Darling did not feel quite the same way. "Six new children is an awfully large number," he said, worried. "It will be very expensive."
"George!" Mrs. Darling cried, upset to see his selfishness come out again.
Then Mr. Darling burst into a smile. He was as glad to have them as she was. "I just thought you could have asked my permission," he said.
The boys all told him that having a father was just as important as having a mother. Delighted, Mr. Darling said that he would find space for them in an extra room.
"We can all fit into a single bed, sir," Tootles assured him.
"Then follow me," Mr. Darling cried merrily. "Mind you, I’m not sure that we have an extra room, but we can pretend to have one." He went off dancing through the house, and the boys danced after him.
As for Peter, before he flew away, he saw Wendy once more. She called to him from the nursery, and he shyly brushed up against the window. "Peter, are you really going away?" she asked.
"Yes, Wendy. It’s time for me to go," he said.
"Peter, don’t you want to ask my parents something?" Wendy asked.
"No, what would I ask?" he answered, trying to sound casual.
Mrs. Darling joined them at the window. When she saw Peter, she told him she would be happy to adopt him as well.
"Would you send me to school?" he asked.
"Yes."
"And then to work?"
"I suppose so."
"Soon I would become a grown-up?" he asked.
"Very soon," said Mrs. Darling.
"I don’t want to go to school, and I don’t want to be a grown-up—ever!" Peter protested. "No one is going to catch me and make me grow up."
"But where will you live?" asked Mrs. Darling gently.
"With Tink, in the house we built for Wendy. The fairies will put it up high among the treetops."
"How lovely," said Wendy longingly.
"I thought all the fairies were dead," said Mrs. Darling.
"There are always more young ones," explained Wendy, who was now an expert on fairies.
"I shall have such fun!" said Peter to Wendy.
"But it will be so lonely in the evenings sitting by the fire," Wendy said sadly.
"Well then, come with me," he said.
"May I, Mother?" Wendy asked.
"Certainly not," Mrs. Darling replied. "You are finally home, and that is where you will stay."
"But who will look after Peter, and cook and clean for him?" Wendy asked. "He does so need a mother."

"So do you, Wendy," said her mother sternly. But when she saw Peter’s mouth tremble, she made him another offer. She would let Wendy join him for one week every year to help him with his spring cleaning.
Having no sense of time, Peter was very happy with this offer. But Wendy said sadly, "You won’t forget me, Peter, will you? Before spring cleaning time comes?"
Peter promised to remember her. And then, in the blink of an eye, he flew away.

Once all the children were settled in at Number 14, Mr. and Mrs. Darling signed the boys up for public school. The boys were in school only a few days before they started wishing they had never left the island of Neverland. But as time passed, they got used to their teachers and to learning everyday things like math and spelling. They settled down and became ordinary boys. No one outside the family ever knew about their magical past.

Sometimes they went back to their old tricks. When no one was looking, they would fly after their hats on a windy day. Other times, they would pretend to fall off the school bus, only to fly safely away. At first, Nana tied their feet to the bedposts, so that they could not fly away at night. But soon they forgot how to fly at all. Maybe it was because they were out of practice. Or maybe it was just that they no longer believed they could.

Being the youngest, Michael continued to believe longer than the other boys. He remembered Neverland for a long time. He was with Wendy when Peter came for her in the spring. Though Peter did not notice, both Michael and his sister had grown much taller. For Wendy, it had been a long wait, and she was excited to talk about the old times. But Peter was carefree as always. He only wanted to talk about his new adventures.
"Who is Captain Hook?" he asked with interest when Wendy mentioned Peter’s old enemy.
"You don’t remember how you killed him and saved all our lives?" she asked, amazed.
"I forget them as soon as I’ve killed them," Peter replied.
When Wendy asked about Tinker Bell, he didn’t know who the fairy was. "Oh, Peter, how could you not remember?" she said in shock.
"There are such a lot of fairies," he said, "and they don’t live too long."
But Wendy still loved Peter. To her, Peter was as fascinating as ever. And when they finally got to Neverland, they had a lovely spring cleaning in the little house in the treetops.
The next year, Wendy waited at the window for days, but Peter did not come for her.
"Maybe he’s sick," said Michael.
"You know he’s never sick," she replied.
Michael came closer and whispered sadly, "Wendy, maybe there is no such person as Peter Pan." Michael burst into tears when he said it. Wendy wanted to cry too.

The following spring, Peter came for her. Strangely, he didn’t remember that he had missed a year. When he brought her back home, he said, "Always be waiting here for me. Some night you will hear my crow. And I’ll be there to bring you back to Neverland!"

That was the last time the little girl named Wendy ever saw him. She tried not to grow up. She tried to be loyal to Peter, but as the years went by, Wendy did grow up, and Peter became a vague memory.

All the boys grew up too. Nibs and Curly became teachers. Michael became an engineer. Slightly married a lady who was a medical doctor and he never had to work again. Tootles became a lawyer and then a judge. The twins owned a shipyard. Like his father, John worked at a bank and couldn’t remember any stories to tell his children. And Wendy got married in a long white dress and became a real mother.

Wendy now had a daughter named Jane, who loved to hear her mother’s stories about Neverland. But most of all, Jane loved hearing about Peter. Wendy had bought her parents’ house, so Jane slept in the same nursery her mother had slept in as a girl. But there were only two beds now—one for Jane and one for her nanny. Once a week, on the nanny’s night off, Wendy would put Jane to bed. Then she would tell Jane wonderful stories about mermaids, fairies, and pirates.
"Tell me about when you were a little girl," Jane would begin sweetly.
"That was a long time ago," her mother would answer.
"Tell me what it was like to fly," said the little girl one night.
"You know, Jane, I can hardly remember. It was a long time ago."
"Why can’t you fly now, Mother?"

"When people grow up, they forget how to fly," Wendy explained. She told Jane about the time Peter flew into the nursery looking for his shadow. "The foolish fellow tried to stick it on with soap and cried when it didn’t work," she said. "But I sewed it back on for him."
"Go on," said Jane impatiently, even though she knew all the stories by now.
"And then he taught us how to fly and we flew to Neverland," said Wendy.
"And what was the last thing he said to you?" asked Jane.
"He told me he would return, and some night I would hear him crowing by the window. But then he forgot all about me," Wendy said with a sad smile.
"Funny, I sometimes hear that crow when I am sleeping," said Jane.

And then one night something unusual happened. It was a spring night, and Jane was asleep. Wendy was in the darkened nursery, sewing in front of the fireplace. Suddenly, she heard a crow. The window blew open and Peter Pan flew in, landing lightly on the floor.
"Hello, Wendy," he said. In the dim light, Peter didn’t notice that she had grown up. As usual, he was thinking mostly about himself.
For a moment, Wendy wished she could be as small as she used to be. "Hello, Peter," she replied.
"Is that John in the bed there?" he asked, pointing to the small body under the sheet.
"No, John is not here now," she said.
Peter looked more closely. "Is it a new one? Boy or girl?"
"A girl," she replied, a bit fearfully.
Peter looked at Wendy. "I’ve come to get you. Have you forgotten? It’s time for spring cleaning!"
She knew it was useless to ask where he had been over the years. Instead she said, "I can’t come with you, Peter. I’ve forgotten how to fly."
"I’ll teach you again," he said.
"Oh, Peter, don’t waste the fairy dust on me. I’ll turn on the light, and you’ll see for yourself."
When she turned on the light, Peter gasped. "You promised not to grow up!" he shouted at her.
"I couldn’t help it," she said. "I’m married now, and this is my little girl in the bed."
Peter sat on the floor and began to weep. Wendy bent down to lift him up in her arms, but Peter backed away. Seeing him so hurt, she left the room sadly.
Peter’s sobs woke Jane. She sat up in bed. "Boy, why are you crying?" she asked.
Peter rose and bowed politely. "Hello, I’m Peter Pan."
"Yes, I know," said Jane. "I’m Jane, and I’ve been waiting for you."
When Wendy returned, she found Peter sitting on Jane’s bed, crowing. Jane was up in the air.
"Jane wants to be my mother," Peter explained.
"He does need a mother," Jane said, flying to his side.
"Yes," Wendy said, "I know that very well."
"He wants me to do his spring cleaning every year," Jane added, rising in the air with Peter.
"Good-bye, Wendy," said Peter, as they headed out into the night.
Wendy rushed to the window crying, "No!" She stood there, watching them fly away together to Neverland, growing smaller and smaller in the sky. "If only I could go with them," she sighed.
